research_interests.research_interest_title: Peatland Mapping and Sensor Fusion
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Diana focuses on scalable mapping and monitoring of peatlands by integrating multiple proximal and remote sensors. She develops hierarchical survey workflows that combine surface covariates (DEM, vegetation indices) with subsurface geophysics (EMI, GPR, resistivity, tTEM) to delineate peat extent, map peat thickness and detect subsidence. Her work emphasizes methodological evaluation and cost-effectiveness, testing which sensor combinations perform best across bogs and fens and under varying field conditions. By fusing airborne/UAV radiometrics with ground-based measurements and targeted field sampling, Diana improves spatial predictions and creates practical guidelines for national inventories. Her applied approach links field-scale studies to broader mapping strategies and produces recommendations that support peatland restoration planning and greenhouse gas reporting.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning for Geospatial Prediction and Uncertainty
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Diana applies and evaluates supervised and unsupervised machine learning methods tailored to geospatial environmental problems. She uses random forests, quantile random forests, multiple linear regression, kriging variants and clustering algorithms (DBSCAN, MCLUST, ISO Cluster) to improve predictions of peat depth, soil properties and GHG proxies. A current focus is Bayesian neural networks to quantify predictive uncertainty and integrate prior knowledge from geophysics and field measurements. She examines how combining surface and subsurface covariates enhances model performance, develops cross-validation and model comparison strategies appropriate for spatial data, and explores ways to turn probabilistic outputs into actionable maps for decision-makers. Her work aims to make ML models robust, interpretable and fit-for-purpose in environmental monitoring contexts.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Applied Geophysics and Radiometric Techniques for Carbon Accounting
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Diana works at the intersection of applied geophysics and carbon accounting, advancing use of portable and airborne radiometric methods to support peatland inventories. She tests portable gamma-ray spectrometry alongside airborne/UAV radiometrics, forward models GPR responses (gprMax) and integrates electrical and electromagnetic surveys to infer peat stratigraphy and organic content. Her research quantifies historical subsidence and long‑term carbon loss, evaluates proxies for greenhouse gas emissions, and recommends sensor-specific workflows for restoration monitoring (hydrology, vegetation, GHG proxies). By linking geophysical measurements to carbon stock estimates and restoration outcomes, Diana provides evidence-based guidance for survey design that balances accuracy, cost, and scalability to inform policy and national GHG reporting.

Contributions.Title: [Remote] Delineation of peatland areas based on drone-borne radiometric surveys and unsupervised machine learning

research_interests.research_interest_title: Practical Machine Learning for Experimental Biophysics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Noah seeks a solid, practical grounding in machine learning methods tailored to experimental biophysics. As a relative novice, he is eager to learn end-to-end workflows: problem formulation, data curation, model selection, validation, and deployment for laboratory use. He is particularly interested in interpretable models, uncertainty quantification, transfer learning from related biological imaging datasets, and strategies for working with small, noisy experimental datasets. Noah also wants guidance on integrating physics-informed priors and constraints into ML models, balancing black-box performance with reproducibility and explainability, and using tools that facilitate collaboration between experimentalists and methodologists. The goal is to leave with concrete, reproducible pipelines and practical heuristics he can apply to his single-molecule biosensing experiments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Image Analysis for Single-Molecule Biosensing
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Noah focuses extensively on image analysis for single-molecule nanowire biosensing and wants to develop ML-based analytical solutions for microscopy data. He aims to master tasks such as spot detection and localization, denoising, segmentation of diffraction-limited signals, and single-particle tracking using convolutional neural networks, U-Nets, and recent self-supervised or physics-aware architectures. Practical concerns include generating realistic synthetic training data, data augmentation strategies for scarce labeled examples, performance metrics appropriate for counting and localization, and strategies for automating annotation pipelines. Noah also wants to learn how to integrate image-derived features with downstream statistical analyses and quality-control steps so that ML outputs can be used confidently in quantitative biosensing studies.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Signal Processing and Statistical Modeling for Nanowire Sensors
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Noah is interested in signal-processing and statistical-modeling techniques for electrical readouts from nanowire single-molecule sensors. He wants to learn practical approaches for time-series denoising, event detection, feature extraction, and real-time classification, together with principled statistical methods for handling correlated noise, missing data, and low-signal regimes. Given his methodological background, Noah is keen to combine classical approaches (filters, spectral methods) with probabilistic models and Bayesian or empirical-Bayes inference to quantify uncertainty and enable robust downstream inference. He is also interested in mixed-effects and joint modeling strategies to account for batch effects, device variability, and repeated-measures designs common in experimental biophysics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Foundation models and Transformers for images and spectra
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Aayush investigates how foundation models and Transformer architectures can be adapted to the analysis of complex imaging and spectral datasets from both laboratory mass spectrometry and astrophysical observations. He is interested in self-supervised and multimodal pretraining strategies that enable transfer across domains (high-resolution MS, chromatography images, telescope spectra) and in fine-tuning pipelines that preserve physical interpretability. Practical targets include automated peak picking and deconvolution, faint-line detection in noisy astronomical spectra, and cross-referencing spectral signatures with network-derived reaction products. Aayush emphasizes rigorous benchmarking against experimental mass-spectrometry datasets (e.g., formose reaction outputs) and observational catalogs, exploring calibration, domain adaptation, and explainability approaches to make Transformer outputs actionable for downstream chemical-network discovery and observational follow-up.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Bayesian optimization for experiment design and instrument tuning
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Aayush focuses on applying Bayesian optimization to efficiently tune instruments and guide closed-loop experiments in both laboratory and observational settings. He aims to reduce experimental resource usage while maximizing information gain: optimizing laser resonance chromatography parameters, mass-spectrometer acquisition settings, and telescope/sensor configurations to improve sensitivity to rare products or weak spectral lines. His interest spans constrained and multi-objective BO formulations (e.g., sensitivity vs. throughput vs. sample consumption), surrogate modeling for noisy and heteroscedastic responses, and integration with automated reaction-network enumeration to prioritize experiments that most increase the probability of discovering autocatalytic cycles or novel compounds. He also studies strategies for transfer learning of acquisition policies across sample types and for combining BO with physics- and network-informed priors.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Deep ensembles for robust uncertainty and discovery in chemical networks
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Aayush is interested in deep-ensemble methods to provide calibrated uncertainties and robust predictions when mining complex chemical reaction networks and observational datasets. He explores ensembles for spectral deconvolution, image classification of chromatographic peaks, and detection of weak astrophysical features, using ensemble variance to flag ambiguous or out-of-distribution cases for experimental validation. By coupling uncertainty-aware predictions with network-centric discovery, Aayush seeks to prioritize candidate reaction pathways or spectral identifications that are both high-value and high-confidence, enabling targeted follow-up. He also evaluates how ensembles combine with Bayesian optimization and physics-based constraints to reduce false positives, support hypothesis testing about emergent autocatalysis, and increase reproducibility when models are deployed across different instruments and observational campaigns.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Colloidal Synthesis and Surface Chemistry of Perovskite Nanocrystals
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Dmitry focuses on controlled colloidal synthesis and surface chemistry strategies for lead‑halide and emerging halide perovskite nanocrystals. His work emphasizes precursor and ligand engineering (including oleylamine purification and I2→oleylammonium iodide routes), shape‑selective methods for producing uniform nanocubes and ultrathin wires, and chemically driven phase transformations such as Cs4PbBr6 → CsPbBr3. Dmitry develops encapsulation approaches—silica and polymer coatings—and automated encapsulation protocols that enable multi‑year aqueous photoluminescence stability. Across synthesis and surface passivation, he combines synthetic innovation with rigorous diagnostics to improve stability, tune optical properties, and translate colloidal materials into device‑relevant forms. This interest spans practical lab protocols, reproducibility, and routes to scale and long‑term material performance in applications ranging from light emission to bioimaging.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Ultrafast Photophysics and Collective Phenomena in Nanocrystal Assemblies
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Dmitry investigates the photophysics of individual nanocrystals and their collective assemblies, exploring exciton dynamics, superradiance, and energy transfer in ordered superlattices and nanoplatelets. He employs advanced spectroscopies—2D electronic spectroscopy, pump–probe techniques—and multilayer diffraction as a laboratory metrology to quantify structural coherence and surface passivation in supercrystals. Research targets include disorder and aging effects, photoinduced halide chemistry in mixed‑halide systems, and interfacial energy transfer to 2D materials such as TMDCs. By combining time‑resolved measurements with structural diagnostics, Dmitry aims to connect microscopic disorder and surface chemistry to macroscopic optoelectronic behavior, guiding design rules for robust, collective photonic materials and improved device performance.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning for Materials Characterization and Lab Automation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Dmitry is beginning to apply machine learning to practical laboratory challenges and materials discovery for perovskite nanocrystals. He works with structured numerical datasets and graph representations, and is particularly interested in transformers and generative models to accelerate interpretation and design. Potential applications include graph‑neural models that map superlattice structure to optical response, generative approaches for proposing ligand or composition variants, anomaly detection and deconvolution in spectroscopy and scattering data, and closed‑loop experimental design for automated encapsulation and stability optimization. As a newcomer, Dmitry seeks feedback on model choices, data workflows, and integration of ML into synthesis and characterization pipelines to make experiments more predictive, reproducible, and efficient.

Contributions.Title: AI/ML Impact Areas in Physics and Materials Discovery of Halide Perovskite Nanomaterials

research_interests.research_interest_title: Multi-scale dynamics of weakly collisional astrophysical plasmas
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Thomas investigates the dynamics of weakly collisional astrophysical plasmas across scales, focusing on how magnetic fields, microscale kinetic processes and macroscopic fluid instabilities interact. He studies instabilities such as the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability, the magneto‑thermal instability and heat‑flux‑driven buoyancy instabilities, and explores kinetic suppression mechanisms driven by whistler and mirror modes. His work synthesizes linear theory and high‑resolution nonlinear simulations to show how microphysical closures alter transport, mixing and dynamo processes in environments from cluster cores to galactic outflows. Thomas emphasises the importance of bridging kinetic physics and fluid MHD to predict observables reliably, and he uses these multi‑scale insights to inform models of conduction, viscosity and composition transport in astrophysical systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Numerical methods, high‑performance computing and community code development
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Thomas develops and applies advanced numerical methods and HPC techniques to study nonlinear plasma dynamics and instabilities. He contributes code development and algorithmic advances across platforms such as Arepo, Athena, Psecas, Paicos and a Vlasov‑fluid PIC code, and implements efficient operators like Braginskii viscosity using super‑time‑stepping on moving meshes. His work couples eigenmode analysis, solver development and scalable postprocessing to enable high‑resolution simulations that resolve both macroscopic instabilities and mesoscopic kinetic effects. Thomas prioritises reproducible, community tools that support diagnostics, benchmarking and cross‑code comparison, helping to make sophisticated multi‑physics simulations accessible to the broader astrophysics and plasma physics communities.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Learning and applying machine learning to astrophysical fluids
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Thomas is keen to learn how machine learning is being used in Denmark and elsewhere to tackle problems in astrophysical fluid dynamics and plasma physics. Although he currently has no active ML project, he is interested in surveying practical applications such as surrogate modelling for expensive simulations, turbulence and transport closures informed by data, emulators for parameter studies, anomaly detection in large simulation/observational datasets, and ML‑assisted analysis pipelines. He is particularly attentive to methods that incorporate physical constraints, quantify uncertainty and preserve interpretability so that ML augments, rather than obscures, physical insight. Thomas aims to connect with practitioners to assess tools, best practices and possible pilot projects that could integrate ML into his multi‑scale modelling workflow.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Analytical and computational approximants for nonlinear dynamics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jonas develops principled analytical and computational approximation methods for nonlinear, out-of-equilibrium systems, with a central emphasis on the BLUES (Beyond Linear Use of Equation Superposition) function method. He extends and adapts BLUES to ordinary and partial differential equations (including second-order time derivatives) to produce rapidly convergent analytic approximants for solitons, wavefronts, interface growth, aeolian dune formation, telegrapher dynamics and reaction–diffusion phenomena. His approach blends asymptotic insight, accelerated convergence techniques and practical numerical validation to yield compact, interpretable expressions that capture both transient and steady behaviour. Jonas values methods that bridge mathematical rigor and experimental relevance, supplying diagnostics and reduced descriptions that guide experiments, provide tight benchmarks for numerics, and enable tractable design and control across soft matter, active systems and biophysical contexts.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Sampling and generation of knotted polymer configurations
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jonas studies the statistical physics and low-dimensional topology of polymers with a focus on generating and characterizing knotted configurations. He combines braid-theoretic/topological diagnostics with stochastic modeling to quantify chirality, aggregation propensity and knotting statistics in confined and interacting polymer systems. A pressing methodological challenge he pursues is improving sampling efficiency for rare, topologically nontrivial states: Jonas is particularly interested in collaborating with machine-learning experts (notably those working on GFlowNets and advanced sampling schemes) to develop generative samplers and annealing protocols that can produce ensembles of strongly knotted configurations with correct weights. His goal is to couple topological invariants, geometric constraints and physics-based priors into sampling algorithms that enable unbiased estimation of knot probabilities, free-energy landscapes, and kinetics in polymeric and biopolymeric systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Thermodynamics, information trade-offs and multi-objective optimization
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jonas investigates fundamental thermodynamic and information-theoretic trade-offs that govern nonequilibrium systems and biological computation. His work derives universal bounds—such as Fano-factor constraints from thermodynamic uncertainty relations—and explores Pareto-optimal fronts for processes like molecular proofreading, heat-engine performance and positional-information encoding in driven reaction–diffusion systems. He combines stochastic thermodynamics with geometric and topological diagnostics to quantify dissipation versus functional accuracy, and to design multi-function optimization protocols that balance competing objectives under physical constraints. Jonas is interested in methods to compute and visualize Pareto fronts, to identify thermodynamically efficient control strategies, and to translate universal bounds into actionable design rules for experiments and synthetic systems across soft matter, active matter and biological contexts.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Generative Neural Networks for Event Simulation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Christian develops and applies generative neural-network architectures to accelerate and complement traditional Monte Carlo event simulation in high-energy physics. Christian explores models such as normalizing flows, score-based samplers, variational autoencoders and GANs to produce particle-level and detector-level events with high fidelity, while paying careful attention to exact symmetries, conservation laws and conditional control over physics labels. Christian is interested in hybrid workflows where learned generators plug into existing simulation chains, in techniques to reduce mode collapse and ensure coverage of rare processes, and in calibration strategies that align neural outputs with full simulation across systematic variations. Christian emphasizes quantitative validation against physics observables and the construction of diagnostics that probe both statistical and physics-driven discrepancies.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Monte Carlo–Machine Learning Integration for Phenomenology
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Christian investigates how machine learning and Monte Carlo tools can be integrated to accelerate phenomenological studies and parameter inference. Christian works on surrogate models for fast likelihood or cross-section evaluation, differentiable emulators for detector response, and neural reweighting / importance-sampling schemes that enable efficient scans of theory parameter spaces and systematic uncertainty propagation. Christian also explores likelihood-free inference (simulation-based inference) techniques to extract posterior distributions for new-physics scenarios directly from simulated ensembles, and studies how learned components can be combined with analytic calculations to preserve theoretical constraints. Christian prioritizes reproducible, modular interfaces that let phenomenologists swap between full MC and ML-based surrogates while tracking fidelity and error budgets for experimental comparisons.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Robust Validation, Uncertainty Quantification and Interpretability
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Christian focuses on robust validation, uncertainty quantification and interpretability of machine-learned models used in particle-physics workflows. Christian develops metrics and coverage tests to quantify where ML surrogates diverge from full simulation, methods for propagating both statistical and systematic uncertainties through learned components, and strategies for domain adaptation when models trained on simulation are applied to real data. Christian further investigates interpretable representations and feature-attribution techniques that expose how models make physics decisions, and constructs ensemble and empirical-Bayes approaches to produce well-calibrated error estimates. Christian values transparent validation pipelines and educational tools that help the community adopt ML methods while retaining rigorous uncertainty control in phenomenological and experimental analyses.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Image Segmentation with U‑Net Architectures
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jack develops and applies convolutional encoder–decoder networks, especially U‑Net variants, for precise image segmentation tasks. He focuses on biomedical and experimental imaging problems where pixel-wise labels and robust boundary detection are critical, tailoring architectures, loss functions (e.g., Dice, focal loss) and multi-scale feature fusion to improve performance on small and imbalanced structures. Jack integrates preprocessing and postprocessing steps, implements quantitative evaluation (IoU, precision/recall curves, calibration), and stresses reproducible training pipelines and model interpretability. His interest spans adapting segmentation models to domain-specific imaging modalities, optimizing inference speed for large 3D volumes, and linking segmented phenotypes to downstream statistical analyses in imaging genetics and experimental datasets.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Robust Data Augmentation and Training Pipelines
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jack studies principled augmentation strategies and end‑to‑end training pipelines to increase model robustness and generalization. He experiments with geometric and photometric transforms, adversarial and synthetic sample generation, mixup and domain randomization, and augmentation policies that respect physical constraints of imaging data. Jack evaluates how augmentation interacts with regularization, batch composition, and class imbalance, and he designs reproducible workflows for large‑scale experiments that include deterministic data versioning, automated hyperparameter sweeps, and uncertainty estimation. Emphasis is placed on practical tooling: containerized experiments, clear documentation, and user‑friendly code so that augmentations and training regimes can be reliably translated into clinical or laboratory practice.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Longitudinal, Missing‑Data Methods and Physics Data Analysis
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jack applies and develops statistical methods for longitudinal, correlated and incomplete data, with an eye toward translating those techniques to experimental physics datasets. Drawing on experience collecting and analyzing data from an IEC fusion reactor, he focuses on mixed‑effects and random‑effects models, EM‑algorithm implementations, selection and mixture approaches for nonignorable dropout, and variance estimation techniques. Jack is interested in robust pipelines for time series quality control, handling structured missingness in sensor arrays, and combining ML‑based feature extraction (e.g., from segmented images) with principled inferential models. He seeks to bridge computer science and physics by producing reproducible software and practical algorithms that support collaborative, data‑driven experimental programs.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Scientific Decisions
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Raphael focuses on interpretable machine learning methods that combine the statistical rigor of classical inference with the flexibility of modern predictive models. He is interested in approaches that provide transparent feature attribution, calibrated uncertainty, and causal or semicausal interpretations suitable for scientific and clinical decision-making. Building on his work with EM algorithms, mixed models, and empirical Bayes, Raphael seeks ML methods that explicitly handle missing and biased data, respect clustered or longitudinal structures, and yield reproducible, well-documented software. He explores hybrid strategies—e.g., interpretable surrogate models, structured regularization, and constrained deep learning—that preserve interpretability without sacrificing predictive performance, and he evaluates them through simulation studies and real biomedical applications to ensure reliability and actionable insights.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Statistical Methods for Longitudinal, Clustered and Genetic Data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Raphael advances methods for complex correlated data encountered in medical, epidemiologic, and genetic studies. His interests include random‑effects and mixed‑model frameworks for unbalanced repeated measures, EM and REML implementations for efficient estimation, generalized estimating equations for correlated binary outcomes, and likelihood and mixture models to address nonignorable dropout. He also develops empirical‑Bayes and nonparametric maximum likelihood techniques for mixing distributions, robust family‑based and haplotype/rare‑variant tests for genetics, and variance‑estimation and bootstrap procedures for valid inference. Raphael emphasizes translating theory into practical, well‑tested software and reproducible workflows so that these methods can be directly applied to problems such as longitudinal biomarker analysis, multi-phenotype genetic association, and meta-analytic synthesis across heterogeneous studies.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Particle and Astroparticle Data Analysis
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Raphael is interested in statistical and computational techniques for particle and astroparticle physics problems such as neutrino oscillation measurements, supernova (SN) searches in astrophysical data, and analyses related to LHC experiments. He applies likelihood‑based inference, mixture models for signal/background separation, and robust handling of missing or censored observations to high‑dimensional detector data and time‑series searches. He is particularly keen on integrating interpretable ML tools and uncertainty quantification into pipelines for discovery and limits, designing analyses that respect experimental clustering and selection biases, and producing reproducible software that bridges methodological advances with domain collaborations in physics. Simulation studies, calibration of test statistics, and clear propagation of systematic uncertainties are central to his approach.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for experimental condensed-matter
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Hippolyte investigates how modern supervised and probabilistic machine‑learning methods can be adapted to support experimental condensed‑matter physics. He is particularly interested in transforming statistical methodology for longitudinal and correlated biomedical data (mixed models, EM algorithms, missing‑data mechanisms) into practical tools for experimenters: robust preprocessing of noisy sensor time series, calibration and uncertainty quantification for high‑throughput measurements, and reproducible pipelines for combining imaging phenotypes with auxiliary metadata. Hippolyte aims to bridge theoretical rigor and experimental constraints — accounting for heterogeneity, nonignorable missingness, and population structure analogues in materials samples — so that ML models produce reliable, interpretable inferences that experimental collaborators can act on and validate.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Reinforcement learning and bandits for adaptive experiments
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Hippolyte explores reinforcement‑learning and bandit frameworks as principled ways to design and control adaptive experiments where measurements are costly and sequential decisions matter. Building on his experience with efficiency, variance estimation and robust inference in longitudinal and genetic studies, he focuses on sample‑efficient policies, exploration–exploitation tradeoffs, and uncertainty‑aware stopping rules that maintain statistical validity. Hippolyte is interested in developing algorithms that respect experimental constraints (limited samples, correlated observations, measurement noise) and provide downstream guarantees for hypothesis testing and effect estimation. His goal is to translate bandit and RL theory into practical adaptive protocols for condensed‑matter labs that accelerate discovery while preserving interpretability and reproducibility.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Clustering and phenotype discovery in noisy high‑dimensional data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Hippolyte is interested in unsupervised learning methods for discovering meaningful subtypes and latent structure in noisy, high‑dimensional experimental data — analogues to his work on SuStaIn and multimarker genetics. He focuses on robust clustering, mixture models, principal‑component aggregation, and methods that explicitly handle correlated measurements and nonignorable missingness. Hippolyte seeks to combine statistical guarantees (stability, variance estimation, empirical‑Bayes adjustments) with scalable algorithms for imaging and spectroscopy, enabling reproducible subtype discovery and downstream association analyses. By adapting phenotype‑aggregation and multimodal integration techniques from epidemiology and genetics, he aims to provide experimentalists with validated, interpretable groupings that reveal mechanistic heterogeneity and guide targeted follow‑up experiments.
